clue.text: Author's upset with hitch over a tropical American tree

indicators.note: in a down clue the first part sits over, above, the rest
in a down clue, upset means the author's name is written upwards, i.e. backwards

parts.note: Kingsley (or Martin) Amis, the English novelist
a rub is a snag or difficulty, as in 'there's the rub'

explanation.surface: A writer is distressed by a problem concerning a tree from the tropics.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns AMIS upwards to SIMA; 'over' puts it above RUB and A in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: Simaruba is a genus of trees native to tropical America, also called paradise tree.

clue.text: Take a secret look around castle

indicators.note: around means the castle word is turned round, read in the other direction

parts.note: a keep is the central fortified tower of a castle

explanation.surface: Someone sneaks a glance about a castle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' looks like it places one thing about another, but here it turns KEEP round.
explanation.definitionFit: To peek is to glance furtively, a direct synonym for a quick secret look.

clue.text: Blimey! TV reveals ladies' clothing

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like blimey
a television set

explanation.surface: An exclamation of shock as a television programme shows women's underwear.
explanation.walkthrough: COR is everyday British slang for an exclamation of surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A corset is a tight-fitting undergarment traditionally worn by women.

clue.text: Upright held by bolts and dolts

indicators.note: held by means the upright word sits inside the bolts word

parts.note: studs are bolts or fastening pins
pi, short for pious, means morally upright

explanation.surface: A vertical post is fastened with bolts by some idiots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upright' reads as a post, but it gives PI (pious), a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Stupids, used as a noun, are foolish people, just as dolts are.

clue.text: Special bitter drink gets things going

parts.note: tart means sharp-tasting, bitter
to sup is to drink, or a sup is a mouthful of drink

explanation.surface: A particular bitter beer livens things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special bitter' looks like a beer name, but splits into S and TART.
explanation.definitionFit: Starts up is a phrasal verb meaning launches or sets in motion.

clue.text: Computerised equipment puts gold in tomato soup

parts.note: Au is the chemical symbol for gold

indicators.note: soup suggests the words are blended into a mixture, rearranging their letters

explanation.surface: Someone drops gold into tomato soup.
explanation.walkthrough: 'soup' looks like the dish being cooked, but it is the signal to rearrange the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Automation is the use of computer-controlled machinery to run processes without people.

clue.text: Catchword wears thin on the radio

indicators.note: on the radio signals that the words are heard spoken rather than read

parts.note: frays means becomes worn and ragged

explanation.surface: A slogan becomes tired from overuse on broadcasts.
explanation.walkthrough: FRAYS and PHRASE are pronounced alike.
explanation.definitionFit: A catchword is a popular saying or slogan, i.e. a set expression.

clue.text: It saves doctor a bit of leg, eradicating the onset of gangrene

indicators.note: to doctor is to tamper with or alter, so the letters are rearranged
the onset of is the beginning, so just the first letter of gangrene is meant

explanation.surface: A medic removes part of a limb to stop gangrene spreading.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters of A BIT OF LEG, less the G of gangrene ('eradicating'), are rearranged by 'doctor'. 'doctor' looks like a person but is the instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifeboat is a vessel used to rescue people at sea, so it is something that saves lives.

clue.text: Reported to be stretched tight, as instructed

indicators.note: reported signals that the word is spoken aloud and heard, not written

parts.note: taut means pulled tight

explanation.surface: Something is said to be pulled tight, as directed.
explanation.walkthrough: TAUT and TAUGHT are pronounced the same.
explanation.definitionFit: Taught is the past tense of teach, so it means instructed.

clue.text: Score book?

definitions.meaning: a grade or point awarded in a test
the Gospel of St ..., a book of the New Testament

explanation.surface: A query about scoring a book, as if rating a novel.
explanation.definitionFit: A mark is a score given for work; Mark is also the second Gospel.

clue.text: Fireworks in the sky make Penny nervous, excited — even gassy

indicators.note: excited means stirred up, so the letters are agitated into a new order
even means the even-numbered letters, the second and fourth, are taken

explanation.surface: A firework display makes a girl called Penny jittery and even flatulent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'excited' rearranges P plus NERVOUS into SUPERNOV; 'even' takes the 2nd and 4th letters of gassy, A and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Supernovas are exploding stars, a fanciful picture of celestial fireworks.

clue.text: Heroine, fair but no saint, covers up deception

indicators.note: covers up means the shortened fair word wraps around the deception word
no means the saint abbreviation is dropped

parts.note: just means fair or equitable
a lie is a deception

explanation.surface: A leading lady is decent but no angel, and she hides a falsehood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no saint' removes S from JUST to leave JUT, which 'covers up' LIE.
explanation.definitionFit: Juliet is the tragic heroine of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet.

clue.text: Can I return? First, run away from helping Trigger

indicators.note: return means the preceding words are sent back, read in reverse

parts.note: a tin is a can
first is number one, I in Roman numerals

indicators.note: away from means the run letter leaves the helping word

parts.note: a ration is a portion or helping
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone asks if they can come back, then flees from an aid that set things off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'return' turns TIN I into INIT; 'First' looks like ordering but is I (one); 'away from' removes R from RATION to leave ATION.
explanation.definitionFit: An initiation is a beginning or setting in motion, as a trigger starts a process.

clue.text: Alarmed, Pluto made move to bite Mickey's bottom!

parts.note: Dis is another name for Pluto, Roman god of the underworld

indicators.note: to bite means the rearranged word closes its jaws around the next letter
move means the letters change places
bottom means the last letter of the name

explanation.surface: Disney's dog Pluto shocks everyone by nipping Mickey Mouse on the behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' rearranges MADE to MAED, which 'to bite' wraps round Y, the last letter of Mickey.
explanation.definitionFit: Dismayed means filled with alarm or distress.

clue.text: Caretaker: "I was taken in by Trojan hoax"

indicators.note: taken in by means the single letter is placed inside the rearranged word
a hoax is a trick, so the letters are mixed up deceptively

explanation.surface: A building's caretaker admits being fooled by the Trojan horse trick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hoax' rearranges TROJAN to JANTOR, and 'taken in by' puts I inside. 'taken in' looks like being fooled.
explanation.definitionFit: A janitor looks after a building, cleaning and maintaining it, as a caretaker does.

clue.text: Building great? Not according to plan

indicators.note: building means constructing something new out of the letters

explanation.surface: A doubter questions whether a construction is impressive and decides it is not as planned.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building' rearranges GREAT and NOT.
explanation.definitionFit: On target is an idiom meaning on course to achieve what was intended.

clue.text: Answer: can son leave bed for fruit?

indicators.note: leave means the son word departs from the jail word

parts.note: can is slang for prison
a cot is a small bed

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a boy can get out of bed to have some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb but is slang for PRISON; 'leave' removes SON to give PRI.
explanation.definitionFit: An apricot is a small orange stone fruit.

clue.text: Dish given to me — let tea be brought out

indicators.note: brought out means the letters are extracted from within the words

explanation.surface: A meal is served to me, and tea should be fetched too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought out' draws the answer from 'tO ME LET TEa', ignoring the dash.
explanation.definitionFit: An omelette is a dish of beaten eggs fried in a pan.

clue.text: Being against Twenty20 and ODI cricket, appeal

parts.note: someone opposed to the short forms of cricket is pro, in favour of, the long form
a Test is a full international cricket match lasting up to five days

explanation.surface: A cricket purist objects to the short formats of the game.
explanation.walkthrough: Twenty20 and ODI (one-day international) are short cricket formats; a fan of five-day Test cricket is PRO-TEST.
explanation.definitionFit: A protest is a formal objection or appeal against a decision.

clue.text: One installed in York, perhaps

indicators.note: installed in means the numeral is set inside the cathedral word

parts.note: York Minster is the great cathedral in York; perhaps marks it as one example of a minster
one is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Someone is appointed to a post at York.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also defines: a minister is a clergyman installed in a church such as York Minster.
explanation.definitionFit: A minister of religion is formally installed in a church post, as at a cathedral.

clue.text: Pressed feed?

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for the metal used in a laundry press, so Fe followed by ed spells this word

explanation.surface: A query whether a pressed garment has been fed.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer as wordplay: the metal's symbol FE plus ED gives FEED.
explanation.definitionFit: Pressed clothes have been smoothed with a hot iron.

clue.text: Rubbish film trip

parts.note: junk means rubbish
ET, the Steven Spielberg film

explanation.surface: A poor movie about a journey.
explanation.definitionFit: A junket is a pleasure trip, often one paid for at public expense.

clue.text: Mourinho's supported by local patriarch

indicators.note: in a down clue, supported by means placed above the next part

parts.note: José Mourinho, the Portuguese football manager
a local is a pub, abbreviated PH for public house

explanation.surface: A football manager is backed by his local community leader.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'local' is British slang for one's neighbourhood pub, abbreviated PH (public house).
explanation.definitionFit: Joseph, son of Jacob, is one of the biblical patriarchs.

clue.text: Indoor court reportedly 88 degrees

indicators.note: in means the court abbreviation goes inside the door word

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: reportedly signals that a word is heard aloud

parts.note: 88 read as eight-eight gives eights

explanation.surface: An indoor sports court reaches a sweltering 88 degrees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Indoor' splits as 'In door', the first part signalling the container. 88 said as 'eight-eight' gives 'eights', which sounds like the ending. The homophone is loose.
explanation.definitionFit: Doctorates are the highest university degrees, such as a PhD.

clue.text: Top 10 record gets a spin

indicators.note: spin means turning around, so the letters are reversed

parts.note: X is ten in Roman numerals
an EP is an extended-play record

explanation.surface: A chart-topping record is played on the radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spin' turns X EP to PEX, following A. 'Top 10' looks like the charts.
explanation.definitionFit: An apex is the highest point or summit of something.

clue.text: Port causes Daily Mail editor to blow his top

indicators.note: to blow his top means losing the top, first, letter of the name

parts.note: Paul Dacre edited the Daily Mail from 1992 to 2018

explanation.surface: Fortified wine makes a newspaper editor lose his temper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Daily Mail is a British tabloid. 'blow his top' looks like rage but removes the first letter, D. 'Port' suggests the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Acre is an ancient harbour city in northern Israel.

clue.text: Enigma's output and what to do with it?

definitions.text: Enigma's output and what to do with it?

parts.words: Enigma's output and what to do with it?
parts.note: the German Enigma machine produced coded messages, which the recipient had to turn back into plain text

explanation.walkthrough: Enigma was the German cipher machine of the Second World War, whose messages were famously cracked at Bletchley Park.
explanation.definitionFit: To decode is to turn a coded message back into readable text.

clue.text: English sailor monkeys about alone

indicators.note: about means turned around, read backwards

parts.note: a tar is a sailor
apes are primates, loosely monkeys

explanation.surface: An English seaman clowns around by himself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'monkeys about' looks like a verb phrase for fooling around; 'monkeys' is a noun and 'about' turns the whole string round.
explanation.definitionFit: Separate means set apart, standing alone and not joined to others.
